claims.text: Increasing noble-metal content enhances the structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic multielement solid-solution nanoparticles at high temperature.
Increasing noble-metal content suppresses thermally induced interdiffusion.
Increasing noble-metal content suppresses elemental segregation.
The compared materials are near-equiatomic multielement solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized identically apart from noble-metal fraction.
Noble-metal content can be varied while all other synthesis parameters and overall composition ratios remain constant.
Temperatures of 773–1173 K represent catalytic service, while 473–1923 K represent thermoelectric service.
Noble-metal content modulates elemental-distribution homogeneity.
Noble-metal content modulates nanoparticle defect structures.
Higher noble-metal content reduces atomic diffusivity.
Higher noble-metal content produces stronger interatomic bonding.
Low atomic diffusion kinetically restrains precipitate formation in multicomponent alloys.
Higher noble-metal content lessens the thermodynamic driving force for interdiffusion and phase segregation.
Suppressing segregation prolongs single-phase stability.
Suppressing segregation increases resistance to precipitation.
Suppressing segregation increases resistance to particle coarsening.
Higher-noble-metal nanoparticles will retain a more uniform elemental distribution than low-noble-metal nanoparticles during high-temperature exposure.
Low-noble-metal nanoparticles are more susceptible to high-temperature phase instability.
Synthesis defects or other dominant factors can diminish the effect of noble-metal content.
The proposed stabilizing trend with increased noble-metal content is supported by analogous alloy studies.
The magnitude and threshold of the proposed noble-metal effect may depend on synthesis and processing variables.

contradictions.description: The noble-metal fraction is to be varied, yet the intervention also says that overall composition ratios will remain constant. Those requirements are incompatible unless 'overall composition ratios' is narrowed to ratios among the non-noble elements.
